title: Sherrelwood well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Sherrelwood wells have a 29 ft median depth and 20 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost and water reliability near Sherrelwood.
h1: Water wells in Sherrelwood and nearby Adams County
intro_html:
Sherrelwood sits on the Denver Basin along the Adams County plains, and most wells around here are surprisingly shallow compared to the foothills and mountains. Records within about 5 miles show thousands of mostly monitoring and domestic wells, so we have a good picture of what depth and yield look like in Sherrelwood, Twin Lakes, Welby, and nearby spots.

If you are buying a place on a well, planning an accessory dwelling, or thinking about a new water supply, it helps to understand how the existing wells in this immediate area are built and performing.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Sherrelwood
sections.html:
The typical well around Sherrelwood is not very deep. The median total depth is 29 feet, and the middle half fall between 20 and 40 feet. About 89% of wells are under 100 feet. Only 4% run 100–300 feet, another 4% are 300–600 feet, and 3% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest on record at 1,751 feet.

That spread tells you two things. Most domestic and monitoring wells here are drawing from shallow alluvial or upper Denver Basin formations. But a small share of very deep Denver Basin completions drives home that you can still hit complex geology. A driller’s bid for a new standard domestic well will usually assume something close to that 20–40 foot band unless you are chasing a specific deeper aquifer.

sections.heading: Well yields and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
On the production side, Sherrelwood’s wells look strong for a plains setting. The median reported pump yield is 20.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half land between 10.0 and 80.0 gpm. About 64% of wells with tests report more than 15 gpm, and another 26% fall between 5 and 15 gpm.

Only 5% of wells are under 1 gpm and another 5% sit between 1 and 5 gpm, so truly low-yield completions are in the minority but they do exist. For a typical exempt household-use well, anything 5 gpm and up is generally workable with storage. At the 10–20 gpm levels that are common here, you usually have plenty of capacity for indoor use and normal irrigation inside the rules, provided the pump, pressure tank, and plumbing are sized correctly.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels around Sherrelwood are shallow. The overall median depth to water is 10 feet below ground, with the middle half between 6 and 20 feet. That means many wells hit water almost immediately after drilling starts, especially in alluvial settings near North Washington, Welby, and Berkley.

The long-term records suggest the water table has not been dropping here in recent decades. Median static level was about 30 feet below surface in the 1960s, improved to 10 feet in the 2010s, and is around 8 feet in the 2020s. That shift toward shallower levels may reflect more monitoring wells and urban recharge, but in practical terms it means short lift distances for pumps and usually lower operating costs. You still want current measurements from the specific well you’re relying on, but there is no broad decline trend showing up in the data.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and when
sections.html:
There is a long history of well construction around Sherrelwood. Within about 5 miles, 10,113 permits show up in the state records, with 5,047 noted as constructed and 5,826 listing a total depth. Permitting ramped up over time: 315 permits from the 1950s, 297 in the 1960s, 200 in the 1970s, then 402 in the 1980s.

Development really took off in the 1990s and 2000s with 1,687 and 1,649 permits respectively, and 2,536 more in the 2010s. Another 987 permits have been issued in the 2020s so far, with the newest in 2025. Most are monitoring wells, but there is still a steady trickle of domestic and irrigation work. The busiest drillers in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 3,353 wells, Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.) with 184, and Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.) with 157.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Sherrelwood
sections.html:
Drilling here is into Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock with some alluvial cover, and local cost models put typical drilling rates around $50–$70 per foot. At the area’s median depth of 29 feet, that means the drilled hole alone pencils out in the $1,400–$2,000 range.

By the time you add steel or PVC casing, grout, a submersible pump sized to your yield, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical work, a finished domestic well in this area commonly falls around $7,400–$14,000. That range assumes depths near the local norm; chasing deeper Denver Basin zones or dealing with difficult access will push costs higher. In a built-up area like Sherrelwood and Twin Lakes, also budget for mobilization, yard restoration, and possible traffic control.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and septic layout
sections.html:
Most Sherrelwood wells are shallow and fairly strong, but there are still risks to look at closely. Around 5% of tested wells make under 1 gpm and another 5% are between 1 and 5 gpm, so a marginal producer is very possible on a given lot. You want recent pump and recovery test data before you buy.

Environmental mapping shows about 699 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 176 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 4 historic mine features within roughly 10 miles. That density means water quality testing is not optional. A basic lab panel should include PFAS screening along with metals and general chemistry. On small parcels in Shaw Heights, Federal Heights, or Berkley, also make sure the well is properly separated from any existing or proposed septic system, and that you have enough space and soil depth for a code-compliant leach field if one is needed.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Sherrelwood well lot
sections.html:
For a lot already served by a well, confirm the permit type, documented depth, and static level. Most local wells are in the 20–40 foot range with around 10–20 gpm yields, but you should verify the actual numbers for that specific permit. Ask for any water-quality lab results, especially given the number of regional PFAS and cleanup sites.

If you are planning new construction, talk with a driller early about which Denver Basin or alluvial unit they are targeting and what they see in nearby completions. Nearly all permitted wells here are tied to Denver Basin aquifers, with many labeled as unnamed or fractured-bedrock and some listed as Alluvial or Quaternary Alluvium. Coordinate the well location with driveway, house footprint, and septic layout so you are not forced into a poor spot later. In this area, paperwork with the Division of Water Resources is straightforward, but you still want everything lined up before you pour concrete.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Sherrelwood, Colorado?
faq.a: State records within about 5 miles of Sherrelwood show a median well depth of 29 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 40 feet. Around 89% of wells are less than 100 feet deep. A small minority are much deeper, including some Denver Basin completions that go several hundred feet and one recorded at 1,751 feet, but most domestic and monitoring wells here are relatively shallow.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Sherrelwood?
faq.a: Reported pump tests show a median yield of 20.0 gallons per minute around Sherrelwood, with the middle half of wells between 10.0 and 80.0 gpm. About 64% of wells produce more than 15 gpm and 26% fall in the 5–15 gpm range. Only about 10% are below 5 gpm, so low-yield wells do occur but are not the norm. For household use, most local wells have ample production if equipped correctly.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Sherrelwood?
faq.a: The data do not show a falling water table. Overall, the median static water level is about 10 feet below ground, with the middle half between 6 and 20 feet. By decade, median depth to water was around 30 feet in the 1960s, 10 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet in the 2020s. That indicates water levels have generally become shallower in this area rather than declining, though you should still check the current level in any specific well you rely on.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Sherrelwood?
faq.a: Local cost modeling for the Denver Basin sediments around Sherrelwood suggests drilling runs about $50–$70 per foot. With a typical local depth around 29 feet, the borehole itself comes to roughly $1,400–$2,000. A complete domestic setup with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals in the $7,400–$14,000 range, assuming average site conditions and no need to chase significantly deeper aquifers.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Sherrelwood?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The area has about 699 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 176 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles, so water quality deserves careful attention. Many domestic wells are used successfully, but you should have a certified lab test for PFAS, metals, and basic chemistry before relying on any well for drinking water, and repeat testing periodically or after any changes in land use nearby.
